readerTitle: Your first store works. Will the second one?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주방용품 매장 1→5호점, 미용실 예약 앱 도시 확장) · 단원 개념 적용 레슨
insight: 1호점이 증명한 것은 '매장 형식'이 아니라 '사장이 있는 매장'일 수 있다. 확장 전에 사장 없이도 돌아가는지 먼저 시험하고, 머릿속 노하우를 가벼운 절차로 옮겨야 한다.
misconception: 1호점이 잘되면 같은 매장을 여러 개 열어도 똑같이 잘된다. 매장을 늘리려면 처음부터 두꺼운 매뉴얼과 큰 시스템이 필요하다.

sources.text: 모든 사례와 장면은 설명용 가상 예시 (실제 수치 없음)

factChecks.note: 이 레슨에는 실제 기업, 연구, 통계가 없습니다. 모든 장면은 가상이며 카드에 illustrative 표시를 했습니다. 게시 전 ENT-06-01(조기 확장)과 ENT-06-04(절차 도입) 레슨의 용어·정의와 표현이 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Your first store works. Will the second one?
body: Maya's kitchenware shop has been busy for three years. Regulars ask her advice by name. Margins are healthy, and a landlord across town offers her a space.
A friend says: why stop at two? Open five. The question is what store one has actually proven.

image.label: One busy shop and four empty storefronts on a map
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 도시 지도 위에 불이 켜진 작은 주방용품 가게 하나와, 불 꺼진 빈 상가 네 곳이 점선으로 연결됨. 가게 안 계산대에 사장이 손님과 이야기 중. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Four spaces are available. What first?
body: Maya has savings and a bank willing to lend. Four landlords will hold spaces for a month. Her current store is profitable and her team is small but loyal.
What should she do before she grows?

options.text: Sign all four leases now, while rents are good
options.feedback: She locks in four sets of rent and staff before knowing if the store works without her. That's **premature scaling**: spending to grow something not yet proven to repeat.

options.text: Open one more store and run it mostly without her
options.feedback: It costs her speed and maybe a good lease or two. In return she tests the real question, whether the format repeats, before betting on five. This avoids **premature scaling**.

options.text: Wait until store one runs perfectly
options.feedback: Store one will never be perfect, and it can't show what happens without Maya in it. Only a second store can answer that.

cards.title: In store one, the owner is the system.
body: Maya orders stock by feel. She knows which regulars want the new knives first. She notices a messy shelf and fixes it before anyone complains.
None of this is written down. It lives in her head and her habits.
So store one's success proves two things mixed together: the shop format, and Maya standing in it. Opening store two pulls those apart. It shows how much of the success travels.

cards.title: Premature scaling, in a shop window
body: **Premature scaling** means spending to grow before the thing you're growing is proven. Leases, staff and stock for five stores are hard to undo.
For Maya, what needs proving is narrow: can a store with her format, but without her, attract and keep customers?
One extra store answers that at the cost of one lease. Five stores answer it at the cost of five.

image.label: One test store versus five stores at once
image.brief: 두 갈래 길 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 길: 매장 1개 → 확인 → 매장 3개. 오른쪽 길: 매장 5개 동시 개점 → 경고 표시. 단순한 아이콘, 로고 없음.

cards.title: Store two is open. It's wobbly.
body: Sales are lower than at store one. Popular items run out. One shift opens late; another gives refunds Maya would never allow.
What should she do next?

options.text: Split her week between both stores and fix things herself
options.feedback: Problems get solved fast, but the knowledge stays in Maya's head. It works for two stores and breaks at five.

options.text: Write simple routines for the few tasks that keep going wrong
options.feedback: An opening checklist, a reorder rule, a refund policy. This is **adding process** where repeated mistakes are costly, while staff keep judgment for everything else.

options.text: Buy a big inventory system and write a full staff manual
options.feedback: It looks professional, but it's costly and slow to learn. **Adding process** too heavily, too early, buries the few rules that matter.

cards.title: Adding process: from head to page
body: **Adding process** means turning what one person does by instinct into routines others can repeat.
Start small. Pick tasks that happen every day and hurt when done wrong: opening, reordering, refunds. Write them on one page each.
Then watch store two. If late openings stop and stock-outs drop, the routine works. If a rule keeps getting ignored, it may be the wrong rule.
list: **Rare or needs judgment:** trust the staff

cards.title: Don't write away what made store one good.
body: Customers loved Maya's shop partly because staff could make small calls, like letting a regular test a pan. Rigid rules can turn a warm shop into a cold chain.
Testing also has a cost. While Maya proves store two, a rival may take the space she wanted. Moving slower is a real price, not a free safety net.
The aim is enough proof and enough process for the next step, not total certainty.

image.label: A one-page checklist next to a friendly shop counter
image.brief: 한 장짜리 체크리스트가 계산대 위에 놓여 있고, 그 옆에서 직원이 손님에게 프라이팬을 건네며 웃는 장면. 규칙과 친절이 함께 있는 느낌. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Now it's a booking app, going from one city to five.
body: Your app lets hair salons take bookings online. In your home city, salons stick with it, largely because the founder sets up each one in person.
Investors want you live in five more cities this year. What's your plan?

options.text: Launch in all five with a big ad budget
options.feedback: Ads bring sign-ups fast, but nobody knows if salons stay without the founder's setup. That's **premature scaling**, and churn may waste the spend.

options.text: Turn the founder's setup into a playbook, test it in one new city, watch retention
options.feedback: Slower to impress investors. But it uses **adding process** to capture the setup, and avoids **premature scaling** by proving salons stay before expanding further.

options.text: Hire five city managers and let each build their own onboarding
options.feedback: Local people help, but five different setups mean five experiments at once, and you can't tell which one works.

cards.title: Prove it repeats, then write down how.
body: You used two ideas. **Premature scaling:** test whether the business works without you before multiplying it. **Adding process:** move the few costly, repeated tasks from your head onto a page.
**Try it today:** list three things you do every week that no one else knows how to do. Write a one-page routine for the one that causes the most trouble when you're away.
